title: Diet Coke Brownies
summary: Cocoa, whey and a can of Diet Coke stirred into a batter and baked with toasted marshmallows on top. Cut into eight squares at about 72 calories each, roughly a quarter of a regular brownie.

time.note: The source gives no bake time - 25 minutes is a starting estimate, not the creator's figure. Go by the doneness test in the method, and let them cool completely before cutting.

nutrition_per_serving.note: One of eight squares. Assumes a zero-calorie granulated sweetener, which is how the source counts it too. Without the marshmallows each square drops to about 60 calories and 0 g added sugar.

ingredients.note: It has to be a dry powder - it is holding the batter together as much as adding protein. Any whey or casein works; Greek yogurt or another wet protein would flood the batter.

The source just says flour, which in a UK or US recipe usually means plain flour (maida) - that works fine. Oat flour, ragi, jowar or almond flour all work too and make it gluten free, oats only if the pack says gluten free.

It has to be a granulated 1:1 sugar replacement: erythritol, allulose, or a granulated monk fruit or stevia blend, gram for gram. At 120 g this is bulk as much as sweetness, which is why drops cannot stand in for it on their own.
If you only have baking soda, use a quarter of the amount. The cola is acidic enough to activate it without adding lemon.
Diet Coke or Coke Zero. It is liquid plus a little lift from the fizz.
They toast and go crisp on top. Most marshmallows contain gelatine, so this is not vegetarian with them in.

steps: Heat the oven to 180C and line a small baking dish with baking paper.
Mix the cocoa, whey, flour, sweetener, baking powder and salt in a bowl. Break up any lumps of cocoa or whey now - they will not dissolve once the liquid is in, and they bake into dry pockets.
Pour in the Diet Coke and stir until just combined. It will fizz. Stop as soon as there is no dry powder left: the bubbles are part of the lift, and beating it knocks them out.
Tip it into the lined dish and level the top.
Bake at 180C until set. The source never gives a time, so start checking at 20 minutes - it is done when the middle no longer wobbles and a skewer comes out with moist crumbs rather than wet batter.
Leave it to cool completely in the dish before lifting it out and cutting into 8 squares. Warm, it is too soft to cut cleanly and the marshmallow drags across every slice.
tips: The marshmallows are the only real sugar in here, about 3 g a square. Leave them off and each square is nearer 60 calories.
No cola? Sparkling water keeps the lift; still water works but the brownies come out a little denser.

The healthiest flours here are the whole grains - atta, oat, ragi or jowar - with about four times the fibre of maida; ragi also has about ten times the calcium of wheat. Almond flour is lower in carbs and bakes fudgier, but adds about 16 calories a square. At 7 g of flour a square, though, none of the grain flours moves the numbers much, so choose on taste. Skip besan, which you can taste, and coconut flour, which soaks up far too much liquid to swap in straight.

Only have monk fruit or stevia drops, or pure stevia powder? They add sweetness and nothing else, and the 120 g they replace is nearly half the dry mix, so it bakes thinner and springier, closer to a sponge. Use what the bottle says matches half a cup of sugar, and a smaller dish so the slab stays thick. A granulated monk fruit or stevia blend swaps in gram for gram instead - most are erythritol underneath.

On the sweetener: the zero-calorie ones add next to nothing to the 72 calories and do not spike blood sugar. Erythritol, the base of most 1:1 blends, is easy on the gut, but a 2023 study of people being checked for heart disease linked high blood levels of it to heart attacks and strokes - an association, not proof. Sugar, jaggery, honey or dates all work, at 40 to 60 more calories and 10 to 15 g more sugar a square, and jaggery is no healthier than white sugar at that amount. Never use aspartame (Sugar Free Gold): it loses its sweetness in the oven.
The dish size decides the bake time more than anything. A bigger dish means a thinner slab that is done sooner, so start checking earlier.

Air fryer: 160C in a tin that fits the basket - a 15-18 cm one takes the whole batch - checking from 15 minutes. If the top sets before the middle, crimp foil over the tin and carry on. Keep the baking paper level with the rim so the fan cannot lift it into the element, and add the marshmallows for the last 3 minutes only, or they scorch.

No oven or air fryer: a kadai or pressure cooker (gasket and whistle out) with a stand inside works as an oven. Preheat it covered on a medium flame for 10 minutes, set the tin on the stand, lid on, lowest flame, and check from 30 minutes. Straight in a frying pan the bottom burns before the middle sets. With no heat from above, the top stays soft and the marshmallows melt rather than toast. For one square, a mug in the microwave works too - check at 45 seconds - but it comes out spongy, not fudgy.
Keep them in an airtight tin for 3 to 4 days. The marshmallow top softens after the first day.
health_notes: About 72 calories and 6 g of protein a square, so a third of the calories come from protein - a good ratio for something sweet, though not much protein in absolute terms. The 63 g of cocoa carries most of the fibre, around 2.5 g a square on its own.

source.title: I Made 73 Calorie Brownies With Coke Zero
source.adapted: Ingredients and method are from the pinned comment. The 180C is from the video at 0:17, since the comment only says bake until set. The video never gives a bake time either - it cuts from the oven door closing to the finished slab - so the 20 minute first check and the doneness test are additions, not the creator's. The sweetener is recorded as a granulated 1:1 replacement, because 120 g only makes sense for one, and the flour as atta, the whole-grain choice, although a UK or US recipe that says flour usually means plain flour. The 73 calories a square holds up at 8 squares, which is how the video cuts it. The device and ingredient alternates in the tips are additions, not the creator's.
